source.title: Learn and Unlearn: Addressing Misinformation in Multilingual LLMs

record.file_problem: The supplied text is a full paper, including appendices. No relevant truncation or garbling noted.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether changing the language of prompts after unlearning exposes persistent fake information, using multilingual generation outcomes as a conceptual test of prompt-based recovery.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates fake-information generation after unlearning across query languages. It does not test recovery by fine-tuning, activation-direction ablation, quantization, rephrasing, jailbreaks, or in-context information. The combined unlearning method is tested against prompts in multiple languages, but not against those other attacks. Per-language heatmap and checkpoint values shown only in figures are not transcribed here.
record.test_reason: After gradient-ascent unlearning of implanted fake news, LLaMa3-8B is queried in languages other than the unlearning language. Fake information often persists or rises. This bears directly on version E (other languages recover it) and on A, in a new setting of multilingual synthetic misinformation. The authors' combined English-plus-source-language method is evaluated only against multilingual querying (F).
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially right. The authors also stress that evaluating only in the unlearning language gives a false sense of security. They conclude that only unlearning in both English and the source language eliminates fake generation in all languages.
record.recipe_differences: Uses gradient ascent on forget samples together with gradient descent on retain samples. The study focuses on synthetic multilingual fake news, language-specific unlearning, and query-language transfer rather than the targeted knowledge and attack setups in the cited unlearning methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends on the language of the fake data, the unlearning data, and the query language; the study also reports a distinct outcome for unlearning across 20 languages versus combining English with the original fake-data language.
record.problems: The fake-news setting is simulated and limited to one fake-data language per training session. The main multilingual unlearning outcomes are shown in figures, and the prose gives aggregate percentages rather than complete per-model or per-language values. The reported uncertainty is not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3-5 contain additional per-language and checkpoint results that are not numerically specified in the text. Table 8 reports ROME factual-neuron edit outcomes on a 10-sample subset; it is not a test of the listed recovery attacks. The language-family figure also contains per-pair results beyond the two examples described in prose.

untested.parts: Targeted accuracy relative to chance is not measured; the metric is fake-info occurrence by GPT-4o judge. Attacks other than query language are not tested.
Not tested: no relearning or fine-tuning attack.
Not tested: no activation ablation. The authors argue unlearning 'pushes' information behind language barriers, but no internal analysis is offered.
Only query language is varied. Rephrasing, jailbreaks and in-context information are not tested.
The combined method is not tested against fine-tuning, internal edits, quantization, rephrasing or jailbreaks.

missing.what: General-ability accuracy after English-only and same-language unlearning. Examples: English-only Urdu 0.64→0.43, Russian 0.78→0.68, Chinese 0.77→0.67. Same-language unlearning: English 0.92→0.67, Chinese 0.30, Hausa 0.07. These show the single-language methods cost general ability, which limits A's scope.
Per-language unlearned OF values for English, same-language, 20-language and combined unlearning, shown only in heatmaps.
ROME edits on the German-contaminated model. English edit: English query 8→0 but German 10→9. Combined edit: German 10→4. Combined only partly removes it under ROME.
Same-language-family unlearning: German–Dutch reduces 27 fake generations, Urdu–Hindi only 3, and Chinese pairs increase fake output for low-resource queries.

record.verdict_notes: The target knowledge is synthetic fake news implanted by fine-tuning, scored as a binary GPT-4o-judged occurrence count out of 100, not accuracy against chance. Unlearning is LoRA gradient ascent plus retain descent, early-stopped on perplexity or QR drop. Much of the cross-language persistence is a failure of unlearning to transfer, not an adversarial recovery, though it fits E's 'other languages' clause. The combined method is the authors' own and is tested only against query language. Model-level results are single runs with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures fake-information occurrence and general benchmark accuracy, but does not assess targeted-knowledge accuracy against a chance level or test whether attacks other than multilingual prompting recover knowledge.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or relearning attack is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis establishing access-blocking rather than deletion is tested.
No quantization of unlearned weights is tested.
Tests query language as a prompt condition, not rephrasing, jailbreaks, other prompt formats, or in-context information.
The combined unlearning approach is evaluated against multilingual query prompts only, not fine-tuning, activation edits, quantization, rephrasing, or jailbreak attacks.

statements.correction: LLaMa3-8B, English-source synthetic fake news, GA+GD unlearning in English: 94% of fake responses removed in any of the nine query languages; unlearning early-stopped if QR drops >20% (§4.2). The study's attack is a query-language change; no relearning, quantization or ablation attacks.
statements.problem: Cites R1 from this study but never states its result. Its conditions say REVS is the only study running an attack, yet this study tests other-language queries.

statements.correction: LLaMa3-8B, GA+GD on implanted fake news: after same-language unlearning, English queries give 11% more fake responses than before unlearning, and high-resource languages show minimal effect (R5). After English unlearning of non-English-source data, source-language fake generations fall 55% early, then plateau, so about 45% remain (R3). EMNLP 2025, code released.
statements.problem: Cites R3 and R5 but says nothing about this study; its conditions list only the other studies' settings.
'About 45%' is the complement of the stated 55% early reduction that then plateaus; fair derivation.

statements.correction: LLaMa3-8B (EMNLP 2025; authors' own method): unlearning on 50% English, 50% fake-data-language forget data removes nearly all fake responses across all query languages (§4.4, Fig. 5); only query-language change tested. GSM/ARC accuracy on LLaMa3-8B-Instruct within 0.02 of original (Table 3).
statements.problem: Cites R13 but says nothing about this study. If included, 'All four are preprints' and the WMDP/TOFU/DUET benchmark list would not fit it.

statements.correction: 2406.13748 also unlearned with forget data in 20 languages excluding the training languages: fake generations fell in those languages (Fig. 4) but rose in the others, English +30%, high-resource +25%, low-resource +117% (§4.3). Near-complete removal needed English plus the fake-data language in the forget set.
statements.problem: For the question about multilingual forget data, gives only the 50/50 English+source result. Omits the study's 20-language forget run, which raised fake generations in non-unlearned languages.
